Chapter 5. Everyday Choices and the Demand for Accountability.
Most of us like to think of ourselves as pretty good people. Maybe you recycle, donate to charity when you can, or just try to be kind. But being good isn’t just about our intentions—it’s really about the choices we make, both big and small, every single day. Sometimes, we don’t even realize just how much those little decisions shape the world around us.
Picture this: you’re scrolling through your social media feed, deciding what to watch or share. Suddenly, a video pops up—it’s funny, but it’s at someone else’s expense. It’s so easy to laugh, hit share, and move on. But here’s something to pay attention to—every click, every share, is like a tiny vote for what we think is okay. Those small choices? They add up.
Accountability isn’t just for politicians or celebrities—it’s for all of us. Think about those moments when someone laughs at a sexist joke, or lets a racist comment slide, or just stays quiet when a friend is hurt. If we let those moments pass, we’re part of the problem, even if we don’t mean to be. It’s not about being perfect—it’s about noticing, and being willing to do better.
Sometimes, we’re tempted to believe that small actions don’t matter. That one person can’t really make a difference. But if you look at culture, it’s actually built from millions of tiny choices like these. When enough people decide that something isn’t funny, or certain behaviors aren’t acceptable, things really do start to change.
Of course, it’s not always easy. Speaking up can feel uncomfortable, or even risky. It might mean losing friends, being called difficult, or just feeling alone in a moment. But silence? That’s its own kind of choice—a way of saying the status quo is good enough.
Real accountability means being honest, even when it’s tough. It means listening when someone tells you they’ve been hurt, instead of getting defensive. It’s about being willing to change, letting go of old habits, and expecting more—not just from others, but from yourself too.
Most people want to believe they’re on the right side. But the real test comes in those small moments when no one’s watching. When you choose to speak up, to listen, or even just to change your mind, you’re helping to build a different story.
And here’s the thing—the demand for accountability isn’t really about punishment. It’s about possibility. It’s about building a world where everyone is treated with respect, where harm isn’t ignored, and where the stories we tell are honest.
Nobody’s perfect. What matters is the willingness to try, to make mistakes, and to keep going anyway. Every choice, even the tiny ones, counts. That’s how change really happens—not all at once, but one decision at a time.
